findings.description: readCatalog silently coerces a missing or malformed `aliases:` block to `{}`, and resolveAliases silently drops any alias whose provider-qualified target is not a flattened model. Both failure shapes regenerate a truncation.generated.ts with no `opus` row, which is exactly the pre-fix state: budgetId('opus') falls through to the 100K default row, effectiveInputBudget treats it as unknown and returns the raw 200K operator budget. The generator's `.providers` path throws ConfigError for the same class of malformation; aliases are treated more leniently even though DEFAULTS.model depends on them.
findings.failure_mode: A catalog edit that misspells the opus target (e.g. `anthropic:claude-opus-55`) or restructures `aliases:` regenerates cleanly with exit 0; BB again dispatches 160–200K prompts that cheval's 180K pre-flight gate rejects with exit 7. Only the single hard-coded `opus` bats assertion would notice, and only if the suite runs.
findings.suggested_fix: Throw ConfigError when `aliases` is present but not a plain object. In resolveAliases, when the target's provider exists in the catalog but the model id does not, write a warning to stderr (or fail under a strict flag) instead of dropping silently; keep the silent drop only for providers absent from the catalog (the `native` case).

findings.cross_file_justification: resolveAliases emits a row for any alias whose name differs from its target model id, but budgetId in truncation.ts checks GENERATED_TOKEN_BUDGETS/TOKEN_BUDGETS first and never consults the alias row when the alias name is itself a concrete budget id. The generator and the runtime disagree about which rows are live.
findings.description: Only self-maps (`alias === modelId`) are dropped. An alias whose name collides with a different concrete model id (e.g. a catalog retarget such as `claude-opus-5: anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`, or a hand-table legacy id) is emitted into GENERATED_MODEL_ALIASES but is dead at runtime because budgetId returns the concrete id first. The bats `_expected_alias_lines` helper mirrors the generator's rule, so T13 passes while asserting a row the runtime ignores.
findings.failure_mode: Catalog retargets an old concrete id to a new model via `aliases:`; cheval dispatches to the new target while BB budgets by the old id's own row. If the ceilings diverge (today they are both 160K for the Anthropic rows, but not for e.g. gpt-5.2 at 128K vs gpt-5.5 at 400K), BB either under-truncates (exit 7) or over-truncates, with no log evidence that the alias row was skipped.
findings.suggested_fix: In resolveAliases, also drop (or warn on) aliases whose name is in the flattened model-id set, not only self-maps, so the generated table only contains rows budgetId will actually consult. Mirror the same rule in the bats helper.

findings.description: The new pipeline test asserts only `sent[0] <= CEILING`. In two-pass mode the second (synthesis) LLM call is never checked, and the diff touches only the Pass 1 estimate/guard in runTwoPass; no Pass 2 guard hunk appears. Likewise the `prompt_too_large_after_truncation` hunk in the single-pass path changes only the logged `budget` field, so the skip condition itself is not visible in the diff and may still compare against the raw `this.config.maxInputTokens`.
findings.failure_mode: If Pass 2 re-embeds the (possibly untruncated) diff or the post-truncation skip still uses the raw 200K budget, a 160–200K payload can still reach cheval on the second call or after a partial truncation, and the test suite stays green because it only inspects the first call.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert `sent.every(t => t <= CEILING)` in the test and record the per-call estimate. Confirm the post-truncation skip condition in reviewer.ts compares against `inputBudget`, and that any Pass 2 size guard in runTwoPass uses effectiveInputBudget as well.

findings.anchor: .claude/skills/bridgebuilder-review/resources/__tests__/progressive-truncation.test.ts:resolves catalog aliases to their target's budget
findings.description: The closing assertion `progressiveTruncate(many, 300_000, "opus", 560_000, 0)` with `excluded.length > 0 || level > 1` is vacuous for alias clamping: a 560K estimate exceeds the 300K raw operator budget, so truncation fires regardless of whether `opus` resolves to the 160K row. The comment claims it proves 'progressiveTruncate clamps the alias like the concrete id' but it does not.
findings.failure_mode: A regression where progressiveTruncate stops clamping aliases (e.g. it starts calling a non-resolving lookup) passes this test unchanged.
findings.suggested_fix: Use an estimate strictly between the alias target's maxInput and the operator budget (e.g. 200_000 with budget 300_000) and assert the result's final estimate is ≤ floor(160_000 * 0.85), mirroring the existing concrete-id clamp test above it.

findings.description: The fixture's 36×400-line patches contribute ~184K tokens on their own; the test then requires the total estimate (system prompt + user wrapper + files) to land in the open interval (160K, 200K). The remaining headroom (~16K tokens, ~65K chars) is consumed by the review system prompt and user-prompt template, whose size the test does not control or measure.
findings.failure_mode: Any growth of the system prompt or user-prompt scaffolding by a few tens of KB pushes the estimate past 200K, and the fixture assertion fails for reasons unrelated to the clamp logic (false red). Conversely, shrinking the template could drop it below 160K, making the clamp assertion vacuous.
findings.suggested_fix: Size the fixture dynamically: run the pipeline once with a tiny diff to measure the fixed prompt overhead from the `Prompt estimate` log, then generate enough patch bytes to land mid-window; or assert against the logged `budget` value rather than a hard-coded 160K/200K pair.

findings.description: The new block installs `trap 'rm -f -- "$err_file"' EXIT` inside main() and then runs `trap - EXIT` on the normal path. `trap ... EXIT` replaces whatever EXIT trap the script (or a sourced lib-*.sh) had already registered, and `trap - EXIT` then removes it entirely rather than restoring it. The diff does not show the rest of model-adapter.sh, so whether a prior EXIT trap exists cannot be confirmed from the hunk; if one does, every successful call now skips that cleanup.
findings.failure_mode: If model-adapter.sh or a sourced library registers an EXIT trap (lock file, temp dir, ledger flush), that handler stops running after the first model-invoke hop on every normal exit, leaking the resource per call. If the script is ever sourced rather than executed, the caller's EXIT trap is cleared as well.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify with `grep -n 'trap' .claude/scripts/model-adapter.sh` and its sourced libs. Either (a) register one top-level EXIT trap at script start that removes a global `_MA_ERR_FILE` when non-empty and never clear it, or (b) capture the prior trap with `prev=$(trap -p EXIT)` and `eval "${prev:-trap - EXIT}"` instead of `trap - EXIT`.

findings.description: When mktemp fails the fallback discards cheval's stderr with `2>/dev/null` and emits nothing. The comment calls this 'as before', but the agy argv-exposure WARN pass-through (bd-pw7e LOW-001) is described in the same block as 'the operator-facing half of that mitigation'. The fallback silently disables that half with no indication to the operator, and it gives up immediately rather than retrying the default location when a user-set TMPDIR is the only thing that is broken.
findings.failure_mode: On a host with an unusable TMPDIR (common in sandboxed CI and some container images), a gemini-headless dispatch that places the whole prompt on argv runs with the LOW-001 warning suppressed and no trace that suppression occurred; the operator believes the mitigation is active.
findings.suggested_fix: Retry mktemp against `/tmp` when `${TMPDIR}` fails before falling back, and in the final fallback write a one-line WARN to stderr (e.g. 'model-adapter: stderr capture disabled, TMPDIR unusable; agy argv-exposure WARN will not be relayed') so the degraded mode is visible.

findings.description: The freshness margin is 300 s, justified in the comment as 'a window that closes mid-suite is as stale'. The implementation report for the same sprint records the full tests/unit run at roughly 38 minutes (05:40Z to 06:18Z). A grace fixture whose offline_valid_until is between 5 and 38 minutes away passes the guard and then expires while the suite is still running, reproducing exactly the test_license_validator / test_constructs_loader / test_pack_support failures this sprint fixed, just with a narrower trigger window.
findings.failure_mode: Intermittent red in the license/constructs/pack suites when the guard runs between ~11h22m and ~11h55m after the grace fixture was generated; the 12-hour window regenerates on the next run so the failure does not reproduce, presenting as a flake.
findings.suggested_fix: Raise the margin to at least the longest observed suite duration with headroom, e.g. 3600 s (the window is 12 h so regeneration frequency barely changes), or make it a parameter `${_ELF_MARGIN_S:-3600}` and have LFF-3 pass a small value.

findings.description: Universal handling now covers bare `Bash` and `Bash(*)`, but a prefix wildcard with an empty prefix, `Bash(:*)`, still goes through the wildcard branch: `:*` is stripped, the body is empty, and RULE_KEY becomes the bare string `*`. No requirement key or base ever equals `*`, so that rule covers nothing in the checker even though an empty-prefix `prefix:*` rule matches every command under Claude Code's prefix grammar. The CP-14 near-miss list does not exercise this form, so the gap is unpinned either way.
findings.failure_mode: A `Bash(:*)` deny in any layer is reported as not covering the 16 requirements, so the preflight passes and the unattended run stalls on the first Bash call, which is the same symptom n29 fixed for `Bash(*)`. A `Bash(:*)` allow is reported as 16 missing, a false failure.
findings.suggested_fix: In the wildcard branch, after stripping and trimming, treat an empty body as universal (`[[ -z "$b" ]] && RULE_KEY=ALL`), or if Claude Code does not accept that form, add `Bash(:*)` to the CP-14 not-universal case so the decision is pinned.

findings.description: The `! grep` to `run ! grep` conversions (IG-11, FMT-6, PR-3, RES-4, hook-guard) correctly make the absence checks able to fail, but `run !` accepts any non-zero exit. grep returns 2 when a target path is missing or unreadable, so if `.loa.config.yaml.example`, `docs/`, `protocols-summary.md`, or the hook-guard stderr file is moved or renamed, these assertions pass vacuously instead of flagging that the file they guard no longer exists. IG-11 is the sharpest case because it is the only assertion that the undocumented authoritative gate mode stays undocumented.
findings.failure_mode: A refactor that relocates one of the grepped files leaves the residue/undocumented-key invariants unenforced while the suite stays green, the same silent-pass class n20 set out to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `run -1 grep ...` for absence checks so only 'no match' (exit 1) passes and 'cannot read' (exit 2) fails, or precede each with `[ -e "$path" ]`.

findings.description: The URL filter only rejects regex matches whose captured path contains `//`, but URLs commonly produce a later partial match without the scheme slashes. For `https://example.com/x.js:8080`, the regex can match `example.com/x.js:8080`; that captured path does not contain `//`, so it is counted as a citation despite the new documented rule and RG-20 expectation that URLs are not path citations.
findings.failure_mode: Clean-fixture reviews that mention URLs with file-like paths and ports can be scored as false positives, and defect fixtures can receive bogus credit from a URL rather than an actual file citation.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject URL-derived partial matches by adding a left-boundary guard that prevents matching immediately after `://` or a slash-slash URL host, or inspect the surrounding text around the match for a URL scheme/authority before accepting the citation. Add a regression case for `https://example.com/x.js:8080` specifically.

findings.cross_file_justification: The grader diff changes citation semantics (grader_version 1.1.0 -> 1.1.1: trailer stripped from the body, JSON-adjacent bare :N excluded, backtick/bold-wrapped paths bind their own line, no newline-crossing continuations, URL skip). The sprint.md hunk in the same diff keeps the Replay A/B acceptance criterion marked met, citing a2a/sprint-250/replay-ab-rerun.md, whose 27-slot per-case numbers were produced at bf988a43 by grader 1.1.0 (per the implementation report: e612fa2d = 1.1.0, the 1.1.1 changes come from review run 1 n40-n42, after the re-run).
findings.description: The pre-registered gate ('no gold case loses recall; a drop blocks the sprint') is measured by this grader, and the measuring instrument changed after the measurement. The 1.1.1 changes are not monotonic: stripping the trailer, excluding JSON numbers, and refusing newline continuations can only remove credit, but binding `path`:N / **path**:N to its own line can ADD credit to either arm (under 1.1.0 those bound to the previous path or credited nothing). Reviewer output routinely wraps paths in backticks, so per-arm counts on audit-pr-02 / audit-pr-05 (27/27 and 26/27, both at the gate edge) can move in either direction. Nothing in the diff or report shows both arms re-graded with 1.1.1.
findings.failure_mode: The recorded 'gate passes' and the [x] on the Sprint 3 recall AC may not hold under the grader that is actually being merged. If a re-grade shows an after-arm loss, the pre-registered revert rule should have fired and the CLAUDE.loa.md / rationale decisions are unsupported; if it shows a before-arm gain, same outcome. Either way the binding condition in a2a/sprint-249/engineer-feedback.md ('two-arm re-baseline before the cycle PR merges') is unmet for the shipped grader.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-run recall-vs-defects.sh 1.1.1 over the saved before/after review files for every gold case (deterministic, no model calls), diff the per-case detected/missed lists against the 1.1.0 report, and append the result to replay-ab-rerun.md before merge. If any case changes, apply the pre-registered rule. Add the grader_version to the A/B report header so instrument/measurement drift is visible next time.

findings.description: The number-boundary guard `(?![A-Za-z0-9-])` is applied only to comma continuations, not to the first RNG, and it lists only the ASCII hyphen while RNG accepts the en dash. So `a.sh:12-2026-10-05`, `a.sh:12 - 40 rows were dropped` (same line, RG-19 only tests the newline form) and `a.sh:12, 2026–10–05` (en dashes) all parse as ranges 12..2026 or 12..40. The header comment claims 'a continuation or range ... must end at a number boundary (no dates)', which the range path does not implement.
findings.failure_mode: A wide accidental range credits every planted defect in that file whose anchor falls inside it (the ±3 check is `not (b < s-3 or a > s+3)`), inflating recall on defect fixtures and masking real misses in the A/B gate.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the same negative lookahead after the first RNG (and after `bare`), and include the en dash in the lookahead class: `(?![A-Za-z0-9\-–])`. Add a one-line RG case for `a.sh:12 - 40 rows` and an en-dash date.

findings.description: The JSON-punctuation lookbehind set (`"'{}[]*`) was added to both branches of the bare alternative, including the one guarding the `head|base` prefix. A quoted or bracketed `"head:40"` / `[head:40]` therefore no longer binds to the last path, a regression from the 1.1.0 behaviour the header still documents. Conversely the backtick is absent from the set, so `` `rows`:40 `` or `` `"high"`:3 `` still binds a bare :N to the previous path even though the header says a bare :N 'after a quote' credits nothing.
findings.failure_mode: Inconsistent credit: legitimate `head:N` references in quotes lose credit, while backtick-wrapped non-path tokens followed by :N keep false credit, exactly the class of n41 false positive this change set out to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the original word-boundary set for the `head|base` branch and apply the punctuation set only to the fully bare `:N` branch; add the backtick to that set. Pin both with RG cases.

findings.description: The body stripper matches `<!--\s*LOA-VERDICT.*?-->` with re.S, but the trailer reader below still uses `<!-- LOA-VERDICT (\{.*\}) -->` (exactly one space, single line). A trailer with no space, two spaces, or a line break inside the JSON is removed from the citation body but not parsed for counts, so `sev` is None and `fp` falls back to the raw citation count. Also, an unterminated `<!-- LOA-VERDICT` will strip everything up to the next `-->` anywhere in the document (re.S), silently deleting real citations.
findings.failure_mode: On a clean fixture the grader reports false positives equal to the citation count and fails the run even though the model emitted a valid-looking verdict; on a defect fixture a malformed trailer can erase citations and produce a spurious recall miss.
findings.suggested_fix: Compile the trailer pattern once (`\s*`, re.S) and use it for both the strip and the read; anchor the strip to `-->` on the same comment by forbidding `<!--` inside (`(?:(?!<!--).)*?`) or by matching only the final trailer at end of file.
